opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be quite skeptical. Benchmarks have been enormously useful in AI. They give the field a shared target and a way to compare systems. But there's a real gap between performing well on a benchmark and having the underlying capability the benchmark was designed to measure.

A few things worry me. First, there's data contamination. These models are trained on vast swaths of the internet, and very often the benchmark items, or things very close to them, are in the training data. So a high score might reflect something more like memorization than reasoning.

Second, even without direct contamination, models are extraordinarily good at picking up on shortcuts, spurious statistical patterns in the data that correlate with the right answer. We've seen this again and again. A system looks like it's doing natural language inference or commonsense reasoning, and then you perturb the problem slightly, change the names, reword it, flip some irrelevant detail, and performance drops dramatically. That tells you it wasn't really understanding the task the way we assumed.

Third, there's what I'd call the anthropomorphism problem. Many of these tests were designed for humans, like bar exams, medical licensing exams, and IQ-style puzzles. When a human passes the bar exam, we make a lot of assumptions about what else that person can do, because human abilities are correlated in certain ways. Those assumptions don't transfer to machines. A model can pass the exam without having the broader competencies we'd infer in a person.

So what would I like to see instead? I think we need to borrow more from cognitive science and developmental psychology, where researchers have spent decades designing careful experiments to figure out what's really going on inside a mind. That means using systematic variations of problems and testing for robustness and generalization, not just accuracy on a fixed set. It means probing whether the system has the right underlying concepts, for instance through analogy tasks like the abstraction and reasoning work I've done. And it means reporting results in a much more granular way, not just a single leaderboard number.

Ultimately, the question isn't "what's the score?" but "what does this score license us to conclude?" Too often, the field has drawn very big conclusions from fairly thin evidence.

r001.rationale: It says models can exploit spurious statistical patterns that correlate with correct answers, so high benchmark scores may not reflect the intended reasoning ability.

r002.rationale: It describes performance dropping after small changes to a task, but does not connect this brittleness to impressive models failing to transition to real-world use.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm fairly skeptical, honestly. I think the first thing to say is that benchmarks in AI have a long history of being, in a sense, "solved" without the underlying capability they were supposed to measure actually being achieved. We saw this with SQuAD for reading comprehension, we saw it with GLUE and SuperGLUE, and now we're seeing it with things like MMLU and the various reasoning benchmarks. A system gets superhuman performance on the test, and then you look more closely and realize it's not doing what a human would be doing to get those scores.

There are a few reasons for that. One is just data contamination. These models are trained on enormous swaths of the internet, and benchmark questions, or things very close to them, are often in the training data. So you can't really tell whether the model is reasoning or retrieving. Another issue, which I think is deeper, is that benchmarks are built around human assumptions. When we give a human a test of, say, analogical reasoning or commonsense physics, we assume that doing well on that test requires certain general abilities, because for humans it does. But that assumption doesn't transfer to systems that learned in a completely different way. A model can find shortcuts, statistical regularities in the way questions are phrased, that let it get the right answer without the capability we care about.

And then there's the question of what "progress" even means. Progress toward what? If the goal is a system that can robustly generalize to novel situations, then a static test score tells you very little, because the whole point of robustness is behavior outside the distribution you tested on. That's why I've argued for things like doing careful variations on tasks, changing surface features while keeping the underlying problem the same, or using counterfactual versions of problems, and seeing whether performance holds up. Often it doesn't. Performance drops in ways that would be very surprising if the system had the general ability the benchmark claims to measure.

So I don't think we should throw out benchmarks, but I think we have to treat them much more like the cognitive scientists treat experiments on people, with controls, with alternative hypotheses, with an awareness of what the system could be doing instead of what we hope it's doing. Right now, a lot of the field treats a leaderboard number as the end of the story, when really it should be the beginning of the investigation.

r001.rationale: The response says models can exploit statistical regularities and shortcuts to get correct benchmark answers without the capability the benchmark is meant to measure.

r002.rationale: It describes brittleness when task variations or counterfactuals are introduced, but does not connect that brittleness to impressive models failing to transition to real-world use.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmarks tell us something, but we have to be careful about what we infer from them. If a system does better on a test, that’s progress on that test. Whether it represents progress toward more general intelligence is a separate question.

With humans, we tend to assume that if someone can pass a difficult exam, they also have a whole collection of more basic abilities. That inference doesn’t necessarily work for language models. They can succeed on something that looks very sophisticated and then fail on a simple variation. So the score alone doesn’t tell us how robust their understanding is.

What I’d like to see is more systematic testing of generalization. If you change the wording, introduce an unfamiliar situation, or alter some detail that matters to the answer, does the system respond appropriately? Can we identify why it succeeds and why it fails? There’s also the question of whether benchmark material appeared in the training data, which can make the results difficult to interpret.

These systems have impressive capabilities. But to understand what those capabilities mean, we need more than a leaderboard. We need experiments that distinguish between competing explanations of their behavior.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether benchmark scores demonstrate general intelligence and mentions possible training-data overlap, but it does not state that statistical shortcuts can produce high scores without the measured ability.

r002.rationale: The response describes failures on simple variations and asks about robustness, but it does not connect brittleness to language models’ limited transition to real-world use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think benchmarks can tell us something useful, but we have to be very careful about what we infer from them. A higher score tells us that a system is better at a particular collection of tasks. It doesn’t necessarily tell us that it has acquired the general ability those tasks were intended to measure.

Take a benchmark that’s supposed to measure reasoning. Humans might need to reason to answer the questions, but that doesn’t mean a language model is arriving at its answers in the same way. There might be shortcuts, statistical cues, or very similar examples in the training data. That makes interpreting the result difficult.

What I’d like to see is more investigation of how robust these abilities are. If you change the wording, introduce an unfamiliar situation, or change something that shouldn’t matter to the answer, does the system still succeed? Can it generalize the underlying idea beyond the particular form in which it encountered it?

These systems have made impressive progress. But I think we need to distinguish progress on benchmarks from progress in our understanding of intelligence. We need evaluations that help us explain both what a system can do and why its abilities break down.

r001.rationale: It says models may use “shortcuts” or statistical cues, so a high benchmark score does not necessarily mean they acquired the intended general ability.

r002.rationale: It raises robustness and breakdowns as evaluation concerns, but does not say brittleness has kept impressive language models from real-world use.
